extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, novelists, and literary critics (readers seeking practical criteria for writing or evaluating novels)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance for producing and evaluating English-language novels (long prose fiction), presented as lecture-notes that isolate major ‘aspects’ or dimensions of the novel and give examples, anti-patterns, and usage guidance. Useful for writers learning craft and critics forming judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: “A fiction in prose of a certain extent” — For the purposes of these lectures any fictitious prose work over 50,000 words will be a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this pragmatic length-based definition to separate short fiction from the novel; the author invites alternative definitions only if they can justify including/excluding borderline works (e.g., Ulysses, The Pilgrim’s Progress).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental aspect — The Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel’s fundamental aspect is its story-telling aspect: the novel must tell a story — the backbone or tape-worm of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize story as the primitive backbone that supplies suspense (the reader’s desire to know ‘what happens next’). Story alone is an ancient, atavistic form and may be insufficient as the highest literary aim, but it is necessary. Use story to create momentum; beware of relying on story alone as the whole of literary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense (what happens next)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping the reader wondering 'what will happen next' is the primary literary tool; Scheherazade’s survival depended on leaving the king at the end of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ suspense deliberately (e.g., strategic pauses, unresolved scenes) as a basic, nearly universal technique. Suspense is distinct from higher artistic aims but essential to hold readers; do not discard it even when pursuing more subtle effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot vs Story (causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the arrangement of events to show causal relations (cause-and-effect), as distinct from story which may be mere sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or constructing plot, ask whether events are connected by causation or merely juxtaposed. Plot implies unity and causal design; a strong plot makes characters’ actions interlock meaningfully rather than merely producing a sequence of incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: People — Characters as essential aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the seven central aspects; novels must present people (characters) with varying degrees of complexity and reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how convincingly characters are portrayed, how they interact with plot and theme, and whether the novelist brings them into being (rather than merely assembling types). The novelist must give characters life and make readers care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round (complex) vs Flat (static) characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters can surprise in a convincing way; flat characters are built around a single idea or conceit and remain consistent but simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for round characters when you want psychological realism and depth; flat characters are valuable when you need an emblematic or dramatic type (they may be easier to sustain over a long plot). Evaluate whether a character’s surprises feel earned (round) or arbitrary (not convincing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view (narrative perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view is a technical aspect that strongly colors a novel; its use (including devices like 'he said' / 'she said') differs across ages and affects tone and intimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and sustain an appropriate point of view; be aware that conventions of reporting dialogue or narratorial intrusion vary historically and will affect readers’ perceptions. Consistency and suitability to material are markers of good technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: personal vs impersonal
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels may employ a personal tone or an impersonal tone; both are valid but produce different effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the narrative voice will be intimate, confiding, and subjective (personal) or more detached and objective (impersonal). Consider which serves the story and characters best; neither tone guarantees genius, but each shapes reader response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy (definition and mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy is an aspect whereby the novelist departs from ordinary reality — exemplified by writers like Sterne and Virginia Woolf — using digression, whimsical objects, and a deliberate bewilderment of direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fantasy when you wish to explore consciousness, comedic bewilderment, or non-linear associative thought. Fantasy techniques include starting from a small object and spiralling outward; they require control to avoid mere ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy (visionary or predictive element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy is the novelist’s capacity to foresee or project social, moral or psychological futures — an aspect distinct from simple realism or reportage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a novel attempts prophetic vision, evaluate its seriousness and grounding: does it illuminate human conditions rather than merely prognosticate? Prophecy is a high aim and may involve philosophical or social insight beyond plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern (external form, unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern denotes an imposed external shape or unity (hour-glass, converging lines, cathedral-like architecture) which can make a work formally beautiful but may shut out the richness of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of rigid pattern: while unity and form can create beauty, an excessive formal pattern can produce artifice and reduce the novel to exercises. Assess whether a chosen pattern arises organically from the material or mutes life for the sake of symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm (internal repetition and variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm (defined in an 'easy' sense as 'repetition plus variation') gives novels beauty from within — e.g., Proust’s recurring ‘little phrase’ — and can stitch a work together without rigid external pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurring motifs, musical phrases, or internal echoes that wax and wane to create surprise and coherence. Avoid turning rhythm into a boring, hardening symbol; rhythm should enliven, not trip up, the reader. Consider both small-scale (motif) and possible large-scale (symphonic) rhythms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring motifs / internal stitching
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrent elements (phrases, images, motifs) that reappear in transformed ways can create internal homogeneity and a sense of beauty (Proust’s Vinteuil phrase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce motifs organically and allow them to vary and reappear in altered contexts; this produces internal binding without externally imposed pattern. Evaluate whether motifs add depth or are merely ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitiveness of the novelist over subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel’s success depends on the novelist’s sensitiveness (the feel of the pen between the fingers), not simply on topical subject matter or historical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the novelist’s perception and tonal sensitivity over topicality. A fresh sensitiveness can make any subject vivid; mere topical relevance (e.g., writing about a current political movement) does not by itself produce a great novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional test — affection for the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The final test of a novel will be our affection for it' — emotional response and attachment are decisive critical measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a novel, measure readers’ affection/engagement alongside intellectual criteria. Beware of allowing sentimentality to dominate judgment too early, but accept that emotional impact is a legitimate and often final arbiter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique of comic/visual detail (cataloguing & visualization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humourists and visualizers (e.g., Dickens, Wells) create effects by cataloguing details and vivid small visual scenes; this produces social commentary and immediate comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use carefully chosen, catalogued details to create humor and social observation. Evaluate whether such catalogues enhance characterization and social insight or merely produce surface liveliness lacking deeper taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding pseudo-scholarship (anti-pattern for criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that classifies novels by crude chronological or topical systems (dates, locality, weather, invented micro-genres) without reading them is pseudo-scholarly and misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a critic or teacher, read attentively instead of imposing tidy taxonomies; do not judge novels primarily by period labels or fashionable categories. For writers: avoid writing to fit a manufactured school rather than to respond to the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius vs Technique (the 'genius' fallback)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pseudo-scholar invokes 'genius' as a catch-all to excuse lack of analysis; genuine achievement combines technique and inventive power, and 'genius' should not be a critical escape-hatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works on observable technique, effects, and achieved sensations rather than simply naming 'genius.' If genius is asserted, seek concrete manifestations (novelist’s control, invention, depth) rather than accepting the label alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual limits and the novelist’s independence
rubrics_metrics.description: While history and subject-matter change enormously, the novelist’s craft and human concerns remain largely constant — 'History develops, Art stands still' — so technique and psychological realism are portable across eras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or judging novels, emphasize timeless craft elements (character, story, rhythm) over merely historical novelty. Historical setting can supply material, but excellence depends on how the novelist processes those facts through imagination and sensitiveness.
